A lengthy post, but I think I followed 100%. You make some great points. There needs to be some kind of impetus or vector for new users to discover that there is a way they're expected to behave (you know... not like a dick) when they're in VRC. This is one way to do it.

I am more than positive that VRC administration is aware of the issues and is actively working on it. I hope they've got the bandwidth to take a breather and read your post in-depth, its a good one that-- while maybe not ever directly implemented as described-- makes a lot of good points about what the community would want this system to provide and do.

Just another thought, after our Endgame trolls episode: We had someone in there who was kind of trolling, and when we confronted him about it he was very upset. He thought he was just being funny. But in the dynamic exchange between the "hosts" of the room/show (us) and him, he learned what behavior was appropriate and changed to adhere to our rules/expectations. Had he just been kicked with a generic warning, or even warned anonymously, the social implication of these anonymous "judgers" might be a very negative/anger-eliciting experience. Trolls are sensitive underneath, and can very easily be motivated down dark paths of revenge/anger (they also happen to be high in psychopathy, according to a recent study: http://www.sciencedirect.com.proxy.library.vanderbilt.edu/science/article/pii/S0191886917304270?_rdoc=1&_fmt=high&_origin=gateway&_docanchor=&md5=b8429449ccfc9c30159a5f9aeaa92ffb&ccp=y )

I am weary of community mods and possible social implications, but 1000x more weary of nasty out of control troll behavior.

I have a bit more power than most in The Pug as it stands, and it makes me uncomfortable wielding it sometimes. I would hope those that are deputized take great care and are held to strict standards of recording incidents just like current VRC mods are.

For a minor example of social dynamics that might be introduced with such a role, consider that a deputized mod would probably have access to all public instances no matter how full they are. This could be used as a social advantage to get friends access to full rooms. Minor things like this along with others can end up adding up to a social dynamic worth considering when it comes to deputized community members.

I'd like to see playermods with no recognition, who have the ability to hide their own avatar and nameplate, mute and globally hide avatars, and make higher priority reports. The playermods who are active, handle valid issues often, and do not abuse power would eventually be eligible to be promoted to a higher mod level, one that has a badge and would be a public presence for encouraging good behavior. The higher tier of mod would have the elevated access with more potential for abuse (seeing player reports, joining on usernames, and ignore room limits).
@{58db230764d6ff1cf2c451c7|full_name}: This sounds a lot like the Janitor system on 4chan, which.. I believe was intended. :)

There's a lot of good research on this subject in the gaming community. Its not the same, but there is overlap. Some things might be easy - like suggestions on the load screen akin to being a better team player could fit here.  It's minor, but easy to implement and hits the issue of fairness when someone is addressed.  A deeper look bigger ideas can be found here:

https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/260663/Video_Reducing_antisocial_behavior_in_games_through_smart_design.php   (this is a GDC talk by Ben, with a PhD in psychology and years of game research exp  :)

also for the old timers... (the fluffy bunny story)

http://habitatchronicles.com/2007/03/the-untold-history-of-toontowns-speedchat-or-blockchattm-from-disney-finally-arrives/

best wishes for the new year

- SteveG  (who had a DK1, left for a while, just came back ... and yes was disappointed by the conversations around me)

The big keyword here for me is visible. That is absolutely the only way any form of community moderation can be down without being a privacy violation in my mind. Finding out that anyone for any reason was banned by a community moderator with no mod status would be something that would push me off this platform.

I am a little late to this, but I just noticed it whilst adding some requests.

I think it's extremely important, given that that the game is non-profit, and has a small team working on it. Bringing Runescape up, I believe that their system actually works fairly well. I have a friend whom actually works on their anti-cheat team and the active player moderators do a very good job keeping the peace when necessary. 

I also believe that player moderators would need a greater level of power in VRChat. This is mainly to deal with those that are abusing the leniency of SDK restriction, anti-cheat etc. Having administrated a Rust server for close to three years now, I understand just how badly one player can affect a playerbase if they aren't dealt with responsibly and correctly.

I'd go as far as saying that although it changes how you play the game, most players would happily take up the responsibility, even if it meant hopping into a world to deal with a "mod request" for 10 minutes. It'd be satisfying know that it's one less person to bump into or ruin the game for others if it's something requiring a temporary/permanent suspension from the game.

I believe that VRChat should remain like the wild west for as long as possible. I am a hacker, and some people want just to see what's possible, and others just want to make people miserable. We should aim to create an environment where engaging in unpleasant acts, entail an unpleasant response, without limiting the freedom and information privacy of creative types like me. I would hate to see this game become overly restrictive, but I also don't like the hushing effect that's causing people to start making private worlds.

In all, aberrant, anti-social, and harmful behavior are 5% in most groups, but their effects are seen by everyone. We should make an infrastructure that limits how they can even harm others in the first place. If someone takes my pen because it's too sharp, I can take a pencil and sharpen it to a shank, if they shorten the pencil, I can take many of them and turn them into little claws. Any tool of any kind can be used to harm others, and trying to take those away won't help, instead we need to make an environment where harm intrinsically is unpleasant. If I'm going to be judged by peers, it doesn't matter if I use a shank, pencil, or even a spoon to harm somebody, I'm going to be judged and there will be consequences of that, which would prevent me from using ANY MEANS of harm to another individual

Community mods has been tossed around a few times, but for now, it isn't a viable solution. Since there has been very little activity on this lately, I'll go ahead and close it.

We are working on ways to improve the ability of users to self-moderate and keep themselves safe while in VRChat, while also improving the effectiveness of our Moderation team.

Hello all! It has been exciting to watch VRChat grow since the days of the Dk2. I’ve had interesting discussions thus far with the VRchat team and community members regarding the possibilities for moderation. I’ve also observed how public rooms have changed as an influx of streamers and new players has increased.

As some of you know, I am getting my PhD in clinical psychology and am learning strategies on how to help people change their behavior. After evaluating behavioral trends of new players in VRChat, I believe it is necessary for an environmental change to elicit a pro-social set of behaviors and foster positive community growth.

I’m going to try to focus on the domains that I believe are most important. I have gone back through to read the previous canny.io mod suggestions to ensure I do not repeat things, and so that I have a better understanding of what has already been suggested. So, to begin I will summarize excerpts of a recent Canny reply post made by Ron:

------
“-Deputizing community members globally is not ideal. At least not in the short term. That would likely remain something we do as a team
-Systems should exist to enable world authors to self moderate alone or with those they choose to deputize. Another set of systems that will help is a more granular social graph including groups, favorites and stats. 
-Tracked user behavior (stats) should also help define how trusted a user is globally. The systems of which would not be fully disclosed much like the real world or online systems such as that used for twitter verification. For example: If someone has 1 friend and has been blocked 20 times in a day and warned by a mod chances are they are trouble vs someone who's made 20 friends, uploaded a world with lots of visits and that we've met and talked to in VRChat.”
-----

Just a note: in my suggestions, by “deputized” I mean mods that are chosen based off some criteria (some of which could be automatic, as mentioned by Ron earlier...e.g., account age). Also, when I refer to “mods” I am referring to non-employee community members; Tupper had a great list of games where this is done (in reference to concerns about mods being employees of VRchat).

(1) Deputized mods can facilitate faster prosocial learning: As new players join VRchat, if they see another player with some kind of “mod” tag, they are presented with the reality that VRchat has a set of rules. Over time players will also get to know the VRchat “commandments.” Mods would politely ask players to change behavior if it’s violating community rules (e.g., “Hey man! Could you cut down on the profanity?”) Compare two new player experiences: 

(A) Player enters the hub and hears someone yelling racial slurs. Nothing happens; player makes assumptions about the entire community of VRchat 
(B) Player enters hub and hears someone yelling racial slurs. A mod walks over to ask the person to stop; when they don’t, they receive a 24 hr public ban
In experience (A) the player learns that it is okay to use profanity. In experience (B), the player is exposed to community rules and learns that when a mod is present, these rules must be abided by.

Just to note - it’s important that these deputized mods are visible to other players. Without this, players may be kicked without being warned beforehand, and other players will not be “influenced” into pro-social norms in the same way. Horrible trolls are created when a player feels they are unfairly banned...if there are some warnings/general social pressure it can help a lot. 


(2) The whole “I want to be a mod” thing can change an entire community: Let’s face it...whenever it’s possible for players to become mods, some people focus on engaging in behaviors to increase those chances. I saw this in Runescape...but it can actually help. Once people seek to become mods, the “guidance” from the VRChat admin team becomes very powerful. People will jump through whatever hoops you create, and you can elicit behavioral control over shaping the VRchat community in the way you want.

(3) Public space in VRChat are inherently different from private ones. The VRChat team had a great update with the “public ban” that emphasizes this difference. It seems the “self-moderation” approach is encouraged at the moment. This may work for invite- or friends-only rooms, but this does not address the “core” of VRChat (public rooms with new users). In these spaces, anyone can join -- we need visual cues of “rule enforcers” who will enforce a fair set of community standards. This will drastically change the experience of public players. 

(4) VRchat is scaling beyond the admin team’s moderation abilities. My real fear of what could happen is the main motivation for writing this post: VRchat is changing and has an organic community. If we do not act quickly enough to shape it the way we hope, it could turn ugly very quickly. The general model of having a VRChat admin in a room for events and such has worked great. 

Lastly, one question that has been contemplated: what if the average troll makes up 50% of the potential VRChat user base? Can these moderation tools/approaches decrease VRchat growth? I propose an answer: if you create the opportunity for private spaces away from “mods” then these “troll” users will have their own places to grow. If they continue to exist in the public spaces, however, you will lose many users who come into VRchat and have negative initial experiences. 

Anyway, those are some of my thoughts about the state of VRchat and our need for public, visible moderators. I’m curious what other people think - thank you for taking the time to read my post!
title: “Deputized” community mods (with a visible label): A needed change for VRchat
